topics.title: Dimensional modeling
topics.about: Grain, fact table types, conformed and special dimensions

items.stem: You're designing a retail sales fact table. The register system records one row per item scanned. Which grain should you declare?
options: One row per item on each receipt
One row per receipt, with its total
One row per store for each day
One row per product for each week
items.why: Start at the most atomic grain the source supports. You can always roll item lines up to receipts, days or weeks; you can never break a daily total back down into items.

items.concept: Keeping one grain per fact table
items.stem: This fact table is one row per order line. Someone added each order's shipping cost to every line. What goes wrong?
options: Summing shipping overstates it
Lines can no longer join to dates
The product key stops being unique
Quantity stops adding up by order
items.why: Shipping cost belongs to the order, not the line, so it repeats on every line and sums to 2x or 3x the real amount. Allocate it across lines, or keep it in an order-grain fact table.

items.stem: Finance wants every account's balance at the end of each month, including accounts with no activity that month. Which fact table fits?
options: A snapshot: one row per account per month
A transaction fact: one row per deposit
One row per account, updated over time
A factless fact: one row per account opened
items.why: A periodic snapshot records the state of every account at a regular interval, whether anything happened or not. A transaction fact only has rows when something happens.

items.stem: You need to track each insurance claim from filed to approved to paid, and report the days between those steps. Which design fits best?
options: One row per claim, updated each step
One row per claim event, never updated
A monthly snapshot of all open claims
A claim dimension with type 2 history
items.why: An accumulating snapshot has one row per claim with a date for each milestone, revisited as the claim moves along. Lags like days from filed to approved become simple column math.

items.stem: Sales and returns are separate fact tables. Leadership wants return rate by product category. What makes that report reliable?
options: Both facts use one conformed product dimension
Both facts are stored in the same database schema
Returns are loaded after sales every night
Each fact keeps its own copy of the product table
items.why: Drilling across two facts works when they share a conformed dimension: same keys, same attribute values. Separate product tables drift, and the categories stop lining up.

items.stem: Why give a customer dimension its own surrogate key instead of using the source system's customer ID?
options: To keep several versions of one customer
To make the table smaller than the source
To hide customer identities from analysts
To remove the need for a date dimension
items.why: A surrogate key lets one source customer have several rows over time (type 2 history), and shields the warehouse from source ID changes or merges across systems.

items.stem: An orders fact has an order date, a ship date and a delivery date. What is the standard way to model these?
options: Join one date dimension three times, by role
Build three separate date dimension tables
Store all three dates as text in the fact
Keep order date; work out the rest in reports
items.why: One physical date dimension plays three roles, usually through views or aliases (order date, ship date, delivery date). It stays consistent and only has to be maintained once.

items.stem: Each order-line row carries the order number. There's nothing else to describe about an order that other dimensions don't already cover. Where should the order number live?
options: In the fact, as a degenerate dimension
In its own one-column order dimension table
In the customer dimension, beside the name
Nowhere; it isn't needed for any analysis
items.why: An order number with no attributes of its own stays in the fact table as a degenerate dimension. It's still useful for grouping lines into orders and tracing back to the source.

items.stem: A sales fact has five yes/no flags: gift wrap, rush, coupon used, online and member. What is a common way to model them?
options: Combine them into one junk dimension
Give each flag its own dimension table
Add all five to the product dimension
Drop them; flags don't belong in a model
items.why: A junk dimension holds the combinations of small low-cardinality flags in one table, so the fact gets one key instead of five, and the flags stay out of unrelated dimensions.

items.stem: You need to record which students attended which class sessions. There is no amount or quantity to measure. What do you build?
options: A factless fact table of attendance events
A student dimension listing their classes
A periodic snapshot of each class's grades
A bridge table between student and teacher
items.why: A factless fact records that an event happened, with keys and no measures. You count rows. A coverage version (who was enrolled) also answers who didn't show up.

topics.title: Change over time
topics.about: Slowly changing dimensions, late-arriving data, effective dating

items.stem: A customer moves from the East region to the West region in March. Region is a type 1 attribute. What does a Q1 sales-by-region report show for this customer?
options: All of Q1 rolls up under West
Jan, Feb East; March under West
All of Q1 rolls up under East
Q1 split evenly across both
items.why: Type 1 overwrites the old value, so history is restated: every past sale now rolls up to West, as if the customer had always been there.

items.concept: SCD type 2: new row per change
items.stem: Same customer, but region is now a type 2 attribute. What does the Q1 sales-by-region report show?
options: Jan and Feb under East, March under West
All of Q1 under West, the current value
All of Q1 under East, the original value
Only March sales; earlier rows are dropped
items.why: Type 2 adds a new row (new surrogate key) when region changes. Sales made before March point to the East version, sales after to the West version, so history stays as it was.

items.stem: Which columns does a type 2 dimension typically add to manage versions?
options: Effective date, end date and a current flag
A created-by user and a last-modified user
A row hash and the source file's name only
A version number for each column that changes
items.why: Effective and end dates say when each version applied; a current-row flag makes "latest version" queries simple. Row hashes help detect changes, but don't manage versions on their own.

items.concept: Joining facts to the right version
items.stem: A sale on March 10 is loaded for customer C-77, whose versions are shown here. Which customer key should the fact row get?
options: 245, the version in effect then
101, the customer's first version
Both keys, one fact row for each
C-77, the ID from the source
items.why: The fact gets the surrogate key of the version whose effective dates cover the transaction date. That's what keeps type 2 history correct.

items.stem: Sales territories are being redrawn once. For a year, leadership wants to see results under both the old and the new territories. Which approach fits best?
options: Type 3: current and prior territory columns
Type 1: overwrite territory with the new one
Type 2: add a new row per changed customer
Type 0: keep the original territory forever
items.why: Type 3 keeps the current value and one previous value side by side, so every row can be reported both ways. It suits a single, planned reorganization, not ongoing change.

items.stem: A customer's credit score at signup should never change, even when the source system updates the current score. How do you treat it?
options: Type 0: keep the original value as is
Type 1: overwrite it with each update
Type 2: add a row for each new score
Type 3: keep the current and prior score
items.why: Type 0 means the attribute is fixed at its original value. The current score, if needed, is a separate attribute with its own type.

items.stem: A support ticket's status changes several times a day, and the business wants average hours between status changes. Where should status changes be recorded?
options: A fact with one row per status change
Type 2 history on the ticket dimension
Type 1 status overwritten on the ticket
A type 3 column with the previous status
items.why: Events you want to measure belong in a fact table (a transaction or accumulating snapshot), not as dimension versions. Type 2 is for descriptive attributes, not workflow timing.

items.stem: A sale from 10 days ago arrives today. Since then, the customer changed region (type 2). Which customer version should the sale join to?
options: The version in effect that day
The current version, as of today
The first version ever recorded
Whichever version was loaded last
items.why: Late facts look up the version effective on the event date, not the load date. Using the current version would put the sale in the wrong region.

items.stem: Orders arrive for a customer who isn't in the customer dimension yet; their details come tomorrow. What is the common approach?
options: Add a placeholder row, update it later
Drop the orders until the customer exists
Load the orders with a null customer key
Hold all of today's orders until tomorrow
items.why: An inferred (placeholder) member keeps the facts loaded with a valid key. When the real details arrive, the placeholder is updated in place.

items.stem: Customer age band and income band change often and are making a type 2 customer dimension grow very fast. What is a common fix?
options: Move them into a mini-dimension
Switch the whole dimension to type 1
Store the bands as text on each fact
Rebuild the dimension once a month
items.why: A mini-dimension holds the combinations of fast-changing bands, with its own key on the fact. The main customer dimension stops churning, and history is still kept.

items.stem: A fact table holds each account's balance at the end of every month. What is the right way to report the Q1 balance for an account?
options: Take the March month-end balance
Add the three month-end balances
Average all of the daily balances
Add January and March together
items.why: Balances are semi-additive: they add across accounts, but not across time. For a period, take the closing value (or an average, if the question is average balance).

items.stem: A table stores each store's conversion rate per day. How do you get one store's conversion rate for the week?
options: Divide total conversions by total visits
Add up the seven daily conversion rates
Average the seven daily conversion rates
Take the highest of the seven daily rates
items.why: Ratios are non-additive. Store the numerator and denominator, sum each, then divide. Averaging daily rates weights a slow Tuesday the same as a busy Saturday.

items.stem: You join these two tables on order_id and SUM(order_total). What do you get?
options: 250, because order A1 is counted twice
150, the true total of both orders
100, because only order A1 matches
200, because each payment row is added
items.why: Order A1 has two payments, so the join returns it twice and its total is summed twice: 100 + 100 + 50 = 250. Aggregate payments to the order grain first, then join.

items.stem: A daily table has unique users per day. Monday shows 800 and Tuesday shows 700. How many unique users were there across both days?
options: Somewhere from 800 to 1,500
Exactly 1,500 unique users
Exactly 750, the average
Exactly 800, the larger day
items.why: People who came both days are counted once per day. Distinct counts can't be added across time; recount from the event level (or use an approximate sketch).

items.stem: A query uses WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM churned), and churned has one row with a NULL customer_id. What does the query return?
options: It returns no rows
Every customer row
Only churned rows
An error message
items.why: Comparing anything to NULL is unknown, so NOT IN with a NULL in the list filters out every row. Use NOT EXISTS, or filter NULLs out of the subquery.

items.stem: A table has 10 rows. The email column is NULL in 3 of them. What do COUNT(*) and COUNT(email) return?
options: 10 rows, 7 emails
10 rows, 10 emails
7 rows, 7 emails
7 rows, 10 emails
items.why: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) skips NULLs. The same rule applies to SUM and AVG, which quietly ignore NULLs.

items.stem: A staging table has several rows per customer_id. You want only the latest row for each customer by updated_at. What is the standard approach?
options: ROW_NUMBER over customer, newest first; keep 1
GROUP BY customer_id and take MAX of each column
SELECT DISTINCT on every column in the table
ORDER BY updated_at and LIMIT the result to 1
items.why: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1 keeps one whole row. MAX per column can mix values from different rows into one that never existed.

items.concept: Filters that undo a LEFT JOIN
items.stem: customers LEFT JOIN orders, then WHERE orders.status = 'shipped'. What happens to customers with no orders?
options: They're dropped, like an inner join
They stay, with NULL order columns
They're counted once with status NULL
They cause the query to return an error
items.why: The WHERE clause runs after the join, and NULL = 'shipped' isn't true, so those customers disappear. Put the condition in the ON clause to keep them.

items.stem: A MERGE into a customer table matches on customer_id. An incoming row's ID already exists, and another incoming row's ID does not. What happens in a typical upsert?
options: One updates; the other is inserted
Both are inserted as brand new rows
Both update existing rows in place
One is skipped; the other updates
items.why: WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT. If the source has two rows for the same key, most engines raise an error, so dedupe the source first.

items.stem: Region A's average order is $50 over 900 orders. Region B's is $100 over 100 orders. What is the average order value across both?
items.why: Weight by orders: (50 x 900 + 100 x 100) / 1,000 = $55. The simple average of the two averages ($75) ignores that region A has nine times the orders.

items.stem: What is the main difference between ELT and ETL?
options: ELT loads raw data first, then transforms it
ELT is only used for streaming data sources
ELT skips transformation of the data entirely
ELT transforms data before it leaves the source
items.why: In ELT, raw data lands in the warehouse or lakehouse first and is transformed there. ETL transforms it on the way in. Both still transform; the order and the place differ.

items.stem: A daily job that appends yesterday's sales fails halfway and is rerun. What makes the rerun safe?
options: Replace that day's data, or MERGE by key
Run the append twice to be sure it lands
Add a retry so it can never fail again
Delete the whole table before every run
items.why: An idempotent job gives the same result no matter how many times it runs. Replacing the day's partition, or merging on a key, means a rerun can't create duplicates.

items.stem: An incremental job pulls rows WHERE updated_at > last_run_time. Some rows commit late with an earlier updated_at. What happens?
options: Those rows are skipped, never loaded
Those rows are loaded twice in a row
The whole job fails with an error
Those rows are loaded on the next run
items.why: A strict high-water mark misses rows that commit after the cutoff but carry an older timestamp. Use a lookback window plus a MERGE on the key, so overlap is harmless.

items.stem: Your incremental load filters the source on updated_at. A customer is hard-deleted in the source. What does the warehouse see?
options: Nothing; the customer stays there
The row is deleted on the next run
The row gets updated_at set to NULL
The next run fails with a key error
items.why: A deleted row has no updated_at to filter on, so timestamp-based loads never see it. Change data capture from the database log, or periodic full compares, catch deletes.

items.stem: You fixed a bug and need to reprocess the last 90 days. What is the safest way?
options: Rerun each day's job, replacing that day
Append the 90 days on top of what's there
Truncate everything and reload all history
Patch the numbers by hand in the gold table
items.why: If daily jobs are idempotent, a backfill is just rerunning them for past dates, each replacing its own partition. No double counting, and other dates aren't touched.

items.stem: The sales job runs at 2 a.m. and the reporting job at 3 a.m. One night sales runs long. What is the better design?
options: Make reporting depend on sales finishing
Move the reporting job to 4 a.m. instead
Run the two jobs in parallel at 2 a.m.
Have reporting retry every five minutes
items.why: Time offsets just hope the upstream is done. A dependency (a DAG edge or sensor) starts reporting only after sales succeeds, and stops it if sales fails.

items.stem: Which failure should a pipeline retry automatically?
options: A brief network timeout to the source
A null in a column that requires values
A source file with a missing column
A duplicate key in the incoming data
items.why: Retries fix transient problems: timeouts, throttling, a busy cluster. Bad data fails the same way every time, so it needs an alert, not a retry loop.

items.stem: A finance dashboard is reviewed once each morning. Source data changes all day. Which approach usually fits?
options: A scheduled batch load before the morning
A streaming pipeline with second-level delay
A manual export whenever someone asks
Querying the source system live each time
items.why: Streaming adds cost and operational work; it pays off when someone acts on data within minutes. A once-a-morning review needs a reliable batch load before people arrive.

items.stem: A message queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. What must the consumer handle?
options: The same event arriving twice
Events that never arrive at all
Events arriving in perfect order
Events losing fields in transit
items.why: At-least-once means no loss, but possible repeats. Deduplicate on an event ID (or make writes idempotent), so a redelivered event isn't counted twice.

items.stem: Mobile events can arrive hours late. Daily totals should reflect when things happened. Which timestamp drives the daily total?
options: Event time, with late data folded in
Processing time, when the row arrived
Load time of the nightly batch job
Whichever timestamp is the later one
items.why: Group by event time so late events land on the day they happened, and let the job update recent days as stragglers arrive (streaming engines bound this with a watermark).

topics.title: Storage and the lakehouse
topics.about: Columnar files, partitioning, Delta, medallion layers

items.stem: Analysts usually read 5 columns out of a 200-column table across millions of rows. Which storage layout suits this?
options: Columnar, so only those columns are read
Row-based, so whole records stay together
One file per row for fast single lookups
Compressed CSV files sorted by the date
items.why: Columnar formats (like Parquet) store each column together, so a query reads only the columns it needs, and similar values compress well.

items.stem: A query filters on order_date = '2026-10-01'. How can a columnar table avoid reading most of its files?
options: Min/max stats per file let it skip files
It reads every file and then filters rows
It caches the full table in memory first
It asks the analyst which files to read
items.why: Parquet and table formats keep per-file statistics such as min and max per column. Files whose range can't contain the value are skipped without being opened.

items.stem: A table was partitioned by customer_id (millions of customers) and queries got slower. Why?
options: Millions of tiny files and folders
Partitions forbid filtering by customer
Customer IDs can't be stored as columns
Partitioning always slows tables down
items.why: High-cardinality partitions create huge numbers of small files, and the overhead of listing and opening them swamps the work. Partition on low-cardinality columns, if at all.

items.stem: A streaming job writes a new small file every few seconds, and reads are getting slow. What is the usual fix?
options: Compact them into fewer, larger files
Add more partitions to spread the files
Convert the table back to CSV format
Delete the oldest files every night
items.why: Compaction (OPTIMIZE in Delta, for example) rewrites many small files into fewer large ones. Reads touch fewer files, and the statistics get more useful.

items.stem: A job is rewriting files in a Delta table while an analyst queries it. What does the analyst see?
options: The last committed version
A mix of old and new files
An error until the job ends
Only rows that haven't changed
items.why: The transaction log records which files make up each version. Readers use the latest committed version, so a write in progress is invisible until it commits.

items.stem: You try to query a Delta table as of three months ago and it fails. What is the most likely reason?
options: Cleanup removed that version's old files
Time travel only works for the current day
The table was never given a primary key
Older versions are kept in a separate table
items.why: Time travel reads old versions through the log, but those versions need their data files. Cleanup (VACUUM) deletes files past the retention period, so old versions stop working.

items.stem: In a bronze, silver and gold layout, what typically goes in silver?
options: Data that's cleaned and conformed
Raw data exactly as it was received
Aggregates built for one dashboard
Archived data older than one year
items.why: Bronze holds raw data as received, silver holds cleaned and conformed data at a useful grain, and gold holds business-level tables and aggregates built for consumption.

items.stem: If you partition a large fact table, which column is usually the best choice?
options: A date most queries filter on
The order ID, which is unique
A free-text product comment
A column queries rarely touch
items.why: Good partition columns have low cardinality and appear in most filters, which is why date is the classic choice. Unique or rarely filtered columns give no benefit.

items.stem: Queries often filter on customer_id, which has millions of values. Partitioning on it is a bad idea. What helps instead?
options: Cluster the data by customer_id
Partition by customer name instead
Create one table per customer
Store customer_id as a text column
items.why: Clustering (Z-ordering or liquid clustering in Delta) co-locates similar values within files, so file statistics can skip most files without a folder per customer.

items.stem: A job tries to append rows with an extra column the table doesn't have. With default schema enforcement, what happens?
options: The write fails until you change it
The extra column is silently dropped
The table quietly adds the new column
The rows are written to a new table
items.why: Schema enforcement rejects writes that don't match the table. Adding the column has to be deliberate, by evolving the schema, so a surprise from upstream can't slip in.

items.stem: Row counts match between source and target, but total revenue is off by 2%. What do you check next?
options: Compare revenue sums by day and key
Rerun the job and compare row counts
Check that the table's columns match
Count the distinct customer IDs only
items.why: Matching counts don't mean matching values. Reconcile the measure itself, broken down by day or key, to find where the difference starts: rounding, currency, filters, or late changes.

items.stem: A dashboard looked fine, but the table behind it hadn't loaded in three days. Which check would have caught it?
options: Alert when the newest data is too old
Check that every row has a primary key
Compare the table to last year's totals
Verify the column types match the source
items.why: A freshness check compares the latest timestamp (or load time) to an expected lag. Stale data often looks perfectly valid, so nothing else catches it.

items.stem: Today's load has 40% fewer rows than any day in the past month, with no errors. What check flags this?
options: A volume check vs a recent baseline
A not-null check on the key column
A uniqueness check on the order ID
A check that the job didn't error out
items.why: A job can succeed and still load half the data. Comparing row counts to a trailing average (allowing for weekly patterns) catches silent drops.

items.stem: After a rerun, revenue doubled for one day. Which test would have stopped it before reaching the dashboard?
options: A uniqueness test on the table's key
A not-null test on the revenue column
A freshness test on the load time
An accepted-values test on status
items.why: The rerun loaded the day twice. A uniqueness test on the grain's key (for example order line ID) fails as soon as duplicates appear.

items.stem: Some fact rows have a product key that doesn't exist in the product dimension. What does that cause?
options: Inner-join reports drop those sales
Reports run more slowly than usual
The product dimension gets new rows
The fact table's grain silently changes
items.why: Inner joins drop orphan rows, so totals shrink without warning. Test for orphans, and point unknown keys at an explicit Unknown member instead of leaving them dangling.

items.stem: The status column should only be open, shipped or cancelled. A new source release starts sending 'SHIPPED'. Which check catches it?
options: An accepted-values test on status
A not-null test on the status field
A row-count test on the whole table
A freshness test on the status table
items.why: An accepted-values test fails on anything outside the agreed list, including case changes, so a quiet source change doesn't split one status into two in every report.

items.stem: Where should a check for duplicate keys run to do the most good?
options: Right after loading, before it spreads
Only in the dashboard, where users look
Once a month, in a separate data audit
Only in the source, before it's exported
items.why: Catch problems at the boundary where data enters (for example bronze to silver) so bad rows are stopped or quarantined before they spread to every table downstream.

items.stem: What is a data contract between a source team and a data team?
options: An agreed schema, meaning and change plan
A legal document about who owns the data
A service-level promise for the dashboard
A list of the users who can query a table
items.why: A data contract spells out the fields, types, meaning and how breaking changes are announced, so a renamed column becomes a planned change instead of a 2 a.m. failure.

items.stem: The share of orders with a NULL discount code jumped from 5% to 60% overnight. Every row passed the not-null rules. What kind of check catches this?
options: A check on the column's null rate
A uniqueness check on the order key
A schema check on the column types
A freshness check on the load time
items.why: Row-level rules can all pass while the overall shape changes. Distribution checks (null rates, averages, category mix) catch upstream bugs that each row hides.

items.stem: Which test failure should stop the pipeline instead of just sending a warning?
options: Duplicate keys in the main fact
A minor rise in late-arriving rows
A rare new value in a comment field
A small change in average order size
items.why: Fail hard on problems that make the numbers wrong (duplicate grain, missing keys); warn on drift that needs a look. If every check fails the pipeline, people learn to ignore them.

topics.title: Metrics and the semantic layer
topics.about: One definition per metric, ratio traps, serving BI

items.stem: Two dashboards show different conversion rates from the same data. What is the most likely first cause to check?
options: They define the denominator differently
One dashboard tool rounds its numbers
The data warehouse is out of disk space
One dashboard uses a different color scale
items.why: Different numbers from the same data usually mean different definitions: sessions vs users in the denominator, different filters, or different time windows.

items.stem: Each region has its own conversion rate. How do you compute the company-wide rate?
options: Total conversions over total visits
The simple average of region rates
The median of the regional rates
The rate of the largest region only
items.why: Compute the ratio from summed parts. Averaging regional rates gives a small region the same weight as a large one.

items.stem: A user can belong to several customer segments. You add up active users per segment. What is wrong with the total?
options: Users in more than one segment count twice
Segments with no users are left off it
The total is correct as long as it's daily
Distinct counts round down by segment
items.why: Overlapping groups make segment counts sum to more than the real total. Show the true total from a separate distinct count, or make segments mutually exclusive.

items.stem: Your warehouse stores timestamps in UTC; the business reports days in New York time. What happens if reports group by the UTC date?
options: Evening activity lands on the next day
Every total is exactly the same anyway
Only weekend totals are affected by it
The warehouse rejects the query as wrong
items.why: Midnight UTC is 7 or 8 p.m. in New York, so the last hours of a New York evening fall on the next UTC date. Convert to the business time zone before taking the date.

items.stem: What is the main job of a semantic layer?
options: Define each metric once for every tool
Store raw data before it is transformed
Schedule the warehouse's nightly loads
Draw charts faster in the BI tool
items.why: A semantic layer holds metric and dimension definitions in one place, so Tableau, notebooks and other tools all compute revenue the same way.

items.stem: Besides the formula, what else must a complete metric definition pin down?
options: Filters, time grain and valid slices
The chart type and its color palette
Which analyst wrote the first query
The size of the table it's built on
items.why: A metric is a measure plus its aggregation, filters (for example excluding test orders), time handling and the dimensions it can be broken down by. Leave any out and two teams will differ.

items.stem: Conversion rose in every region this month, yet the company-wide rate fell. How is that possible?
options: Traffic shifted toward low-rate regions
The regional numbers must be miscounted
The company rate must have a rounding bug
Conversion always moves in opposite ways
items.why: Mix shift: if more traffic comes from regions with lower rates, the overall rate can fall even while each region improves. Always check mix before reporting a trend.

items.stem: Headcount was 100 on January 1 and 120 on January 31, and it rose steadily. What is January's average headcount?
options: About 110 over the month
Exactly 220, the two added
Exactly 120 at month-end
Exactly 100 at the start
items.why: Headcount is a point-in-time measure. Month-end and average headcount answer different questions; label which one a report uses.

items.stem: A Tableau dashboard is slow because it scans an event-level table with billions of rows. What usually helps most?
options: A gold table at the dashboard's grain
A bigger cluster that runs the same scan
An extract refreshed every five minutes
Removing the date filter from the view
items.why: Build a gold table (or aggregate) at the dashboard's grain, such as daily by product and region, with conformed dimensions. The dashboard reads thousands of rows instead of billions.

items.stem: Last week's revenue changed after it was presented, because late transactions arrived. What is the best practice?
options: Label numbers with an as-of date
Hide the late transactions forever
Never update numbers after Monday
Report only rounded revenue figures
items.why: Late data is normal. Show when a number was pulled, and decide on purpose whether a period is open or closed, so restated figures don't look like errors.
